meta.chapterLabel: Lesson 12: Asking about Places: What Is at Nikko?

items.scene: naming where something exists, with あります (arimasu) or います (imasu)
items.note: This is the location-of-existence use of に, paired with あります/います. The same に particle already marked direction with いきます (Lesson 6), a point in time (Lesson 7), and the person an action is directed at (Lesson 9) — here it just marks where something exists.
items.reviewNote: Possibly already taught — already introduced in Lesson 2: Possession: Whose Pen Is This? (matched on target)

items.scene: introducing something new, in a 〜があります (~ga arimasu) existence sentence
items.note: Marks a newly introduced subject, or one the speaker believes is new information to the listener — used after a noun with あります/います. Same が already met as が (but), joining two contrasting clauses (Lesson 11); here it has nothing to do with contrast, it simply marks the subject.
items.reviewNote: Possibly already taught — already introduced in Lesson 6: Going Places (1): Where Are You Going? (matched on target) | Excluded as a duplicate of chapter-6/ga-particle, which teaches the same word with the same meaning and is the earlier occurrence.

items.scene: about a thing being in a place
items.note: Used for inanimate things (books, buildings, trees). Compare います (be, exist), used for animate things — people, animals, insects.
お is an optional honorific prefix; the bare root is てら. This chapter's dialogue uses the お-prefixed form.
items.reviewNote: Source shows this headword as "(お)てら" with the prefix in parentheses.

items.scene: listing a couple of things and implying there are others
items.note: Connects two or more nouns while implying other unlisted things also exist, e.g. おてらや じんじゃが あります (there are temples, shrines, and more). Contrast と (and), which implies nothing else exists.
items.reviewNote: Possibly already taught — already introduced in Lesson 9: Doing Things (2): Do You Often Come Here? (matched on target)

items.note: 〜って なんですか repeats part of what you just heard to ask what it means.
items.reviewNote: Placeholder 〜って なんですか filled with おんせん — this is literally how the chapter's own dialogue uses the pattern.
items.target: おんせんってなんですか

items.english: Emphasis particle (calls attention to new information)
items.note: Added to the end of a sentence to call attention to information the speaker thinks the listener doesn't already know.

items.scene: pointing at a photo of an onsen on a smartphone
items.note: Worked example of よ, added because the speaker thinks this is new information for the listener.

items.english: There is a reception desk on the first floor.
items.reviewNote: Deliberately diverges from the book, which glosses うけつけ as "information desk" here. The deck teaches インフォメーション = "Information desk" as its own card, so that English is an ambiguous Production prompt; chapter 1 defines うけつけ as "Reception desk" and chapter-13-extras already uses that wording. Do not revert to match the source.
items.target: 1かいにうけつけがあります
items.ttsText: いっかいにうけつけがあります

items.note: Used for animate things. Compare あります (be, exist), used for inanimate things — books, buildings, trees.

items.hint: the full phrase, as it's commonly said for "woman"
items.note: おんな (female, woman) + ひと (person) = おんなの ひと. Compare おとこの ひと (man).

items.hint: the bare root word, not the full phrase for "woman"
items.note: The root of おんなの ひと (woman) — usually said as the fuller おんなの ひと rather than alone.

items.english: There is a woman at the reception desk.
items.reviewNote: Deliberately diverges from the book, which glosses うけつけ as "information desk" here. The deck teaches インフォメーション = "Information desk" as its own card, so that English is an ambiguous Production prompt; chapter 1 defines うけつけ as "Reception desk" and chapter-13-extras already uses that wording. Do not revert to match the source.
items.target: うけつけにおんなのひとがいます

items.note: Position word. Pattern: noun 1 (thing/place) の noun 2 (position) — e.g. テーブルの うえ (on the table).

items.reviewNote: Excluded as a duplicate: chapter-10 already teaches はな with the identical gloss "Flower", and both cards carried the same id (hana-flower), which collided when the book package maps each card id to one Anki note. The backward de-dup flagged this at build time as already introduced. The earliest occurrence is kept; the WORD POWER hotel-room list simply re-uses the word.

items.english: There are flowers on the table.
items.target: テーブルのうえにはながあります

items.english: At Nikko, there are temples, shrines, and other sights.
items.target: にっこうにおてらやじんじゃがあります

items.english: There is a bank and a convenience store on the first floor (and nothing else).
items.note: Uses と, not や — と implies nothing else is there besides the bank and convenience store, unlike や which implies other things too.
items.target: 1かいにぎんこうとコンビニがあります
items.ttsText: いっかいにぎんこうとコンビニがあります

items.hint: the full phrase, as it's commonly said for "man"
items.note: おとこ (male, man) + ひと (person) = おとこの ひと. Compare おんなの ひと (woman).

items.note: The root of おとこの ひと (man) — usually said as the fuller おとこの ひと rather than alone.

items.english: What is there on the first floor?
items.ttsText: いっかいになにがありますか

items.scene: answering what is on the first floor

items.note: そば (soba, buckwheat noodle) + や (shop suffix) = そばや. This や is a different word from the や (ya) particle meaning "and, and so on" taught earlier in this lesson — here it attaches to a food name to mean "the shop that sells it."
Root word inside そばや (soba shop).

items.english: What is near the Japanese inn?
items.reviewNote: Possibly premature — explicitly taught later in Lesson 13: Asking for a Place: Where Is It? (built on ちかく, which reappears in a dedicated vicinity/location vocabulary list (この ちかく), suggesting it's formally retaught rather than just reused)
items.target: りょかんのちかくになにがありますか

items.english: There are a big lake, waterfall, and other things.
items.scene: answering what is near the Japanese inn
items.target: おおきいみずうみやたきがあります

items.reviewNote: Possibly premature — explicitly taught later in Lesson 13: Asking for a Place: Where Is It? (ひきだし is explicitly re-taught as a dedicated office-supplies vocabulary entry)

items.note: Pattern: だれも + negative verb = "no one (is/does...)". Compare なにも ありません (there is nothing), the same pattern with なに instead of だれ.
items.reviewNote: Excluded at the audio review: the target was the book vocabulary list's SCHEMATIC pattern (… and 〜 are placeholders for a verb), so it is not an utterance. Its audio was meaningless, its romaji unreadable, and its Production face unanswerable. The pattern is taught concretely by だれもいません and なにもありません in this same lesson, and this card's だれも/なにも comparison moved onto だれもいません.
Possibly premature — explicitly taught later in Lesson 13: Asking for a Place: Where Is It? (built on ひきだし, which is explicitly re-taught as a dedicated office-supplies vocabulary entry)
items.target: ひきだしのなかになにがありますか

items.scene: answering what is in the drawer
items.note: なにも + negative verb = "nothing". Compare だれも…〜ません (no one), the same pattern with だれ instead of なに.

items.english: Who is in the next room?
items.target: となりのへやにだれがいますか

items.scene: answering who is in the next room
items.note: だれも (dare mo) with a negative verb means "no one." Same frame as なにもありません (nani mo arimasen, "there is nothing"), with なに (nani) in place of だれ (dare).

items.english: On Sunday, I'm going to Hakone by car.
items.note: くるまで uses で to mark the means of transportation — "by car."
items.target: にちようびにくるまではこねにいきます

items.note: どこ alone (Lesson 5) simply asks "where"; adding の to get の どこですか asks for a more specific place within a larger area already named — here, exactly where in India.
